alt: A schematic shop front with signage and lighting, window displays and landscaping. Storefronts signal the type of shop and prices; window displays attract attention; landscaping makes the exterior inviting. Mower et al. (2012) linked landscaping and window displays to greater liking, which is linked to intentions to visit.
caption: An attractive exterior increases liking, which links to intentions to shop.

alt: Earlier studies found classical music led to dearer wine and national music boosted that country's wine, suggesting priming. Study card for North et al. (2003): on different evenings a restaurant played classical, pop or no music; spend per head was highest with classical music. Evaluation covers ecological validity, lack of random allocation, generalisation and consent.
caption: Classical music evenings brought the highest spending per head.

alt: Woods et al. (2011) found loud background noise lowered ratings of sweetness and saltiness but raised ratings of crunchiness. Three suggested reasons are attention drawn away from taste, arousal or discomfort, and masking or enhancing the sounds of eating. Food in aircraft and noisy restaurants may need stronger seasoning; the laboratory method was controlled but artificial.
caption: Noise weakens sweet and salty tastes but makes food seem crunchier.

alt: Environmental stimuli such as music, light, scent and crowding produce three emotional states: pleasure, arousal and dominance. These lead to approach behaviours (staying longer, exploring, spending, returning) or avoidance (leaving, not returning). A pleasant, moderately arousing environment where shoppers feel in control encourages approach.
caption: Stimuli shape pleasure, arousal and dominance, which drive approach or avoidance.

alt: A pleasant scent improved shoppers' perceptions of the mall and of product quality, which were linked to spending. The real mall gives ecological validity, but questionnaires are subjective and people differ in which scents they like.
caption: Scent works through perceptions of the mall and its products.

alt: Two schematic shop interiors: human crowding with too many people, and spatial crowding with too much merchandise or too little space. Crowding reduces dominance, so shoppers feel less in control and less satisfied, but the effect depends on expectations: a crowded market can be enjoyed while the same crowd in a boutique feels unpleasant.
caption: Crowding lowers dominance, but expectations decide how much it matters.

alt: Four suggestions for a bookshop, each linked to a concept: a freeform layout with seating for browsing, slow quiet music for pleasure and moderate arousal leading to approach, a subtle pleasant scent, and uncluttered aisles to avoid spatial crowding and keep a sense of dominance.
caption: Link each design choice to the concept that predicts it will work.
